questions.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (3x-4){e}^{-3x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x-4\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-3x}\, & ⟹\,v=-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (3x-4)\cdot {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =(3x-4)\cdot (-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3})-\int (-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3})\cdot 3\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3x-4){e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{(3x-4){e}^{-3x}}{3}+\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{(3x-4){e}^{-3x}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}+C \\  & =-\frac{(3x-3){e}^{-3x}}{3}+C \\  & =(1-x){e}^{-3x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.

We need to express $\int 6x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 6x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =6x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 6\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =6x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-6\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-6(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))+C \\  & =6x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+6\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x{csc}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={csc}^{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cot}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ where $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{csc}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-2x} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3x\cdot {e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x & =3x\cdot (-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2})-\int (-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2})\cdot 3\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3x{e}^{-2x}}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}3x{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{3x{e}^{-2x}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{0}+\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3x{e}^{-2x}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{0}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-2x}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[0{e}^{-2(0)}-(-1){e}^{-2(-1)}]-\frac{3}{4}[{e}^{-2(0)}-{e}^{-2(-1)}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[0+{e}^{2}]-\frac{3}{4}[1-{e}^{2}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2}-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}({e}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & ⟹\,v=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\cdot \frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\int (-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+{\frac{1}{5}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5})|}_{0}^{\pi /5} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\frac{1}{5}\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)]+[\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[-\frac{\pi }{25}\cdot (-1)+0]+[0-0] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{25}.\end{aligned}
$$
